interactionPlan.concept: How a pinhole aperture selectively filters light rays to form a sharp, inverted image of a scene on a sensor.
learningObjectives: Understand how a scene point projects light rays in all directions (light spray)
Explain how an occluder with a pinhole filters these rays to establish a 1:1 mapping between scene locations and sensor locations
Describe why the projected image on a camera sensor is spatially inverted relative to the scene
Analyze the trade-off between aperture size, image brightness, and blurriness
interactionPlan.keyInsight: Without an occluder, every point on the sensor would receive light from every point in the scene, resulting in a blank white blur; the pinhole acts as a selective filter that allows only one ray per scene point to pass through.

interactions.label: Scene Position (n)
interactions.effect: Moves the active emitting light source along the scene array, changing which light rays are projected through the pinhole onto the sensor.
interactions.teaches: Demonstrates the geometric inversion of the image (left-to-right mapping) and the point-to-point correspondence.

interactions.label: Aperture Width
interactions.effect: Widens the pinhole gap in the occluder, allowing a cone of multiple rays from the active scene point to pass through and spread across several sensor pixels.
interactions.teaches: The trade-off between sharpness and brightness: a wider aperture lets in more light (brighter) but blurs the image by spreading one scene point across multiple sensor pixels.

interactions.label: Show Blocked Rays
interactions.effect: Toggles the visibility of the light rays that are blocked by the black occluder wall.
interactions.teaches: Emphasizes that the scene is constantly radiating light in all directions, and the camera works primarily by blocking/discarding unwanted rays rather than focusing them.

demo_steps.title: Tracing a Single Light Ray
demo_steps.narration: Look at the red pixel at position 2 in the scene. Notice how it radiates a 'spray' of light in all directions, but the black occluding barrier blocks almost all of them. Only a single ray aligned with the narrow pinhole passes through to strike the camera sensor at index 2.
demo_steps.focus: The pathway of the unblocked red ray going from scene position 2, through the pinhole, to sensor position 2.

demo_steps.title: Observing Spatial Inversion
demo_steps.narration: Move the scene position slider to the right (e.g., to position 10). Notice how the ray passing through the pinhole now crosses over to land on the opposite side of the camera sensor. This geometric crossing-over is why pinhole cameras produce physically inverted images.
demo_steps.focus: The physical crossing of the ray at the pinhole, demonstrating why the sensor's coordinate system (n) is flipped relative to the scene.

demo_steps.title: The Purpose of the Occluder
demo_steps.narration: Toggle off the blocked rays to see only the light that actually reaches the sensor. Without the occluder, all the rays you saw in Step 1 would flood the sensor, overlapping and washing out any image. The occluder is crucial because it filters out the chaotic mix of overlapping light.
demo_steps.focus: The clean, isolated single ray reaching the sensor when blocked rays are hidden.

demo_steps.title: The Cost of a Wider Aperture
demo_steps.narration: Now, widen the aperture. Observe how a cone of multiple light rays can now pass through the gap. While this makes the image brighter by letting more light in, the light from our single scene point now spreads across multiple sensor pixels, causing the image to lose its sharpness and become blurry.
demo_steps.focus: The spreading/widening footprint of the light rays striking the camera sensor as the aperture size increases.

interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: The visualization should consist of three main horizontal layers: a 'Scene' grid at the top labeled 'l_w' with indices 0 to 12 left-to-right; a black 'Occluder' bar in the middle with a central gap ('Pinhole'/'Aperture'); and a 'Camera sensor' grid at the bottom labeled 'l_s' with indices 12 to 0 left-to-right (flipped). The active scene pixel is highlighted in red, emitting red ray vectors. Rays that hit the black bar terminate there (colored dim red/gray if 'showAllRays' is true, or hidden if false). Rays passing through the aperture continue to the sensor, illuminating corresponding sensor pixels in red.
